text:
Count every word in Jane Austen's Emma, and rank them from most common to least. Top of the list is the little word to, five thousand two hundred and thirty-nine times. On plain axes, the counts fall off a cliff. And then the ranks just keep going, all the way out to seven thousand and seventy-nine. More than half of those words lie flat along the floor. They're used once or twice. Now switch both axes to a log scale, where each step is ten times the last. The curve straightens into a line. That straight line is Zipf's law. It's one over the rank: go ten times further down the list, and a word turns up a tenth as often. That's a slope of minus one, and Emma's first thousand words come out at minus one point one.

So the law makes a prediction. The second word should turn up half as often as the first, and the tenth word a tenth as often. In Emma, the second word, the, turns up five thousand two hundred and one times. It nearly ties with to. And the tenth, she, comes in at more than four times its prediction. The law is rough at the very top.

Log axes show the shape, but they're bad at shares. On a log rank axis, the top hundred words fill half the width. On a plain one, they're one point four percent of the vocabulary. Count what they fill, though, and those hundred words are sixty percent of the book. And of its seven thousand and seventy-nine different words, thirty-nine percent appear only once.

That lopsided split is why stopwords exist: a few words fill most of the text, and they say the least about it. Seventy of Emma's top hundred are on NLTK's stopword list. And it's why IDF gives a word more weight the rarer it is.
